score_meanings.app_protocol_promise_semantics: 0 uses command/request-response-service/permission framing or needless pCID fragmentation, 5 models storage, computation, send/receive, reciprocal promises, local trust, make/break evidence, and payload kinds under stable protocol pCIDs where appropriate
score_meanings.envelope_discipline: 0 ignores the settled envelope direction or confuses pCID with payload/message/request identity, 5 aligns with grid([42(pCID), payload, ...]), stable Protocol-CID semantics, and protocol-owned later slots
score_meanings.kernel_implementation_promises: 0 treats the kernel as RPC authority, service registry, capability registry, permission issuer, or generic conformance judge, 5 names local app/kernel promises, assumptions, unsupported behavior, and observations
score_meanings.promise_vocabulary: 0 drifts into claims/profiles/generic statement capsules/central trust-ledger/RPC/service-registry/capability-table or per-message-pCID framing, 5 stays promise-first, layer-local, and pCID-specific
score_meanings.simplicity_durability: 0 overbuilt, selector-shopping, mode-matrix/service-catalog/capability-map heavy, per-record-pCID fragmented, or fragile, 5 minimal, durable, and small-device-friendly under the 100-year goal

promise_theory_rules: A promise is a scoped declaration of intent.
No agent can make a promise on behalf of another agent.
Trust is a local assessment of whether a promise will be kept.
Promises to receive or use are not equivalent to obligations, impositions, or promises to give.
promise_theory_references: Mark Burgess, In Search of Certainty
Mark Burgess, Promise Theory: Principles and Applications

assessment.rationale: Strong PromiseGrid-aligned envelope and local promise-accounting design. It cleanly reframes app/kernel support as local promises plus local observations, avoids registry/RPC authority drift, and uses one stable protocol pCID with payload kinds appropriately. It fits the kernel-porting-boundary scenario well at the app/kernel boundary, but it does not fully specify the broader first-port promise surface for storage, networking, keys, lifecycle, and checkpoint duties that the scenario also pressures.
strengths: Excellent envelope discipline around CBOR grid([42(pCID), payload, ...]) and protocol-owned later slots.
Promise-first vocabulary is consistently local, scoped, and non-authoritative.
Observation records distinguish refused, not-promised, broken, timed-out, unreadable, and host-unavailable outcomes clearly.
Single stable protocol pCID with payload kind variants is simple and evolution-friendly.
Kernel implementation promises are framed as best-effort delivery and local evidence, not registry or capability authority.
weaknesses: Scenario coverage is narrower than the full porting-boundary pressure; many kernel/runtime roles remain intentionally deferred.
Implementation guidance for multi-service split kernels and very constrained hosts is still high-level.
The protocol is still draft-status and leaves some retention/bounds details to future specs.
risks: Broader porting audiences may still want a more explicit split between provisional kernel promises and higher-layer app/storage/network protocols.
The draft title and examples center on app/kernel receive-handle behavior, which may underspecify other porting-role promises unless extended carefully.
If local adapter wrappers are documented poorly, implementers could regress toward hidden RPC semantics despite the stated boundary.
open_questions: What is the minimum guide-facing kernel/runtime promise set before DR-davod freezes broader porting obligations?
Should broader kernel roles such as networking, keys, lifecycle, and checkpoint reconstruction stay in this same payload family or move to separate higher-layer protocols?
What bounded evidence-retention promises are realistic on very small hosts without weakening later auditability?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; supports local app/kernel promise-accounting and envelope choices, not a final kernel API or frozen porting obligations.

autonomous_agents.note: Apps, kernels, peers, and observers each promise only their own behavior.

scoped_intent.note: Promises are relationship-scoped, pCID-scoped, role-scoped declarations of intent.

no_promises_for_others.note: The kernel does not certify app abilities; it records what the app promised and what it observed.

no_guaranteed_outcomes.note: Kernel behavior is best-effort and outcomes are recorded as observations rather than guaranteed facts.

local_trust_assessment.note: Observation records are explicitly local evidence for local trust updates, not global authority.

accept_use_not_obligation.note: Receive/handle promises and receiver behavior are kept distinct; acceptance is not framed as obligation.
